text: Dive log, Tuesday. We dropped into the sunny shallows just after lunch, and within five minutes Tully spotted a cuttlefish hovering above the sand. frame: Commander Rhee's log from the space station has been beamed to the Soggy Biscuit's radio.
text: Station log, day forty-one. This morning we passed over the middle of Australia just as the sun came up, and I floated by the window for the whole twelve minutes it took to cross. From four hundred kilometres up, the desert looked enormous and completely empty, a rusty brown that stretched from one edge of the window to the other. Then I spotted the river. It is one of the longest rivers on the continent, thousands of kilometres from end to end, yet from up here it wound across the desert like a loose thread dropped on a brown carpet. It was a thin, dark green line, curling back on itself again and again, and in places it almost disappeared. I tried to photograph it, but the camera kept focusing on a smudge where my nose had touched the glass. My crewmate Jo says I spend more time at the window than at my experiments. She is probably right. Tomorrow we pass over the reef, and I have already cleaned the glass. Jo has asked me to stop pressing my face against it, but I can't promise anything. The reef is meant to be the best view of the whole mission, and I don't intend to miss a second of it.

frame: Poet Pip has pinned this concert review to the Mirage Mangroves noticeboard.
text: The Mangrove Youth Orchestra played its end-of-year concert on Saturday night, in a tent pitched right on the edge of the mudflats. It was a bold choice of venue. Halfway through the first piece, the tide came in, and the cellists had to lift their feet onto their chairs. Nobody stopped playing. The highlight was a new piece called Storm Over the Channel, written by the orchestra's youngest member, a Year 6 student named Felix. It began with the violins playing so quietly that the notes were as faint as a mosquito in the next room. Slowly the drums joined in, and the whole tent seemed to tremble. By the final minute, the brass section was blasting out notes like foghorns across the bay, and a family of egrets took off from the trees in alarm. When the last note ended, there was a moment of complete silence. Then the audience burst into applause that drummed on and on, like heavy rain on a tin roof. Felix bowed three times and then, to everyone's delight, fell off the stage into the mud. The mud washed off his suit eventually, but the story will last a lot longer. He has already asked for three copies of this review.
